simple: The distance light travels in one year — used because space distances in kilometers get unwieldy.
technical: Approximately 9.46 trillion km (5.88 trillion miles), derived from the speed of light (≈299,792 km/s) multiplied by the number of seconds in a Julian year.

simple: Another unit for measuring huge distances in space, slightly larger than a light-year.
technical: Defined via stellar parallax: the distance at which 1 astronomical unit subtends an angle of one arcsecond. 1 parsec ≈ 3.26 light-years ≈ 30.9 trillion km.

simple: A giant cloud of gas and dust in space — some are stellar nurseries where new stars form.
technical: An interstellar cloud of hydrogen, helium, and dust. Emission nebulae glow from ionized gas; reflection nebulae scatter starlight; dark nebulae block light behind them.

simple: An extremely bright, distant object powered by a supermassive black hole feeding on surrounding matter.
technical: Short for 'quasi-stellar radio source' — an active galactic nucleus where infalling matter in an accretion disk around a supermassive black hole radiates enormous energy across the spectrum.

simple: A spinning neutron star that sends out regular beams of radiation, like a cosmic lighthouse.
technical: A highly magnetized, rapidly rotating neutron star that emits beams of electromagnetic radiation from its magnetic poles, observed as regular pulses when the beam sweeps past Earth.

simple: A planet that orbits a star other than our Sun.
technical: Detected primarily via the transit method, radial velocity, direct imaging, or gravitational microlensing. Over 5,000 have been confirmed as of the mid-2020s.

simple: A swirling disk of gas and dust spiraling into a massive object, like water circling a drain.
technical: Material orbiting a massive central body (a black hole, neutron star, or protostar) that gradually spirals inward, heating up via friction and gravitational energy release, often emitting intense radiation.

simple: The 'point of no return' around a black hole — past it, nothing, not even light, can escape.
technical: The boundary in spacetime beyond which gravitational pull exceeds the speed of light's ability to escape, defined by the Schwarzschild radius for a non-rotating black hole.

simple: Light stretching toward the red end of the spectrum as its source moves away from us — used to measure how fast galaxies are receding.
technical: A shift of spectral lines toward longer wavelengths, caused by the Doppler effect (relative motion) or cosmological expansion of space itself. Higher redshift generally indicates greater distance.

simple: A massive, explosive death of a star — briefly outshining an entire galaxy.
technical: Occurs when a massive star exhausts its nuclear fuel and its core collapses (Type II), or when a white dwarf in a binary system accretes enough mass to trigger runaway fusion (Type Ia).

simple: The incredibly dense collapsed core left behind after a massive star explodes as a supernova.
technical: A stellar remnant composed almost entirely of tightly packed neutrons, typically about 20 km across but more massive than the Sun — a teaspoon of its material would weigh billions of tons on Earth.

simple: An invisible form of matter that doesn't emit or reflect light, but whose gravity shapes galaxies.
technical: Inferred from gravitational effects — galaxy rotation curves, gravitational lensing, and large-scale structure — that can't be explained by visible matter alone. Its exact physical nature remains unknown.

simple: A mysterious force that appears to be accelerating the expansion of the universe.
technical: Inferred from observations of distant supernovae showing the universe's expansion is accelerating rather than slowing. It is estimated to make up roughly 68% of the universe's total energy content, but its physical nature is unknown.

simple: The range of distances from a star where a planet could plausibly have liquid water on its surface.
technical: Also called the 'Goldilocks zone' — depends on stellar luminosity and temperature. Being in the habitable zone is necessary but not sufficient for habitability; atmosphere, magnetic field, and other factors matter too.

simple: Analyzing light from an object to determine what it's made of, how fast it's moving, and more.
technical: The study of how matter absorbs and emits electromagnetic radiation. Each element produces a unique pattern of spectral lines, allowing astronomers to determine composition, temperature, velocity (via Doppler shift), and more from light alone.

simple: How fast an object is moving toward or away from us, measured by the stretching or squeezing of its light.
technical: One of the primary exoplanet detection methods — a planet's gravity causes its host star to wobble slightly, producing a periodic Doppler shift in the star's spectral lines that reveals the planet's presence and minimum mass.

simple: The speed an object needs to break free of a planet's (or star's) gravity without further propulsion.
technical: Derived from energy conservation: v_escape = √(2GM/r). For Earth, it's about 11.2 km/s at the surface.

simple: Spinning in the opposite direction to most other objects in the Solar System.
technical: Most planets rotate counterclockwise as viewed from above the Sun's north pole; Venus and Uranus are notable exceptions, likely due to ancient collisions or tidal effects.
